headings: 5.5 WORK DONE BY A VARIABLE FORCE
pages.page_summary: This page discusses kinetic energy and work done by a variable force. It includes a table of typical kinetic energies for various objects, a worked example (Example 5.4) calculating the emergent speed of a bullet, and a derivation of work done by a variable force using the limit of a summation to a definite integral. A graph (Fig. 5.3(a)) illustrates the concept of work as the area under a force-displacement curve.
knowledge_points: Kinetic energy is the capacity of an object to do work by virtue of its motion.
Table 5.2 lists typical kinetic energies for objects like a car, running athlete, bullet, stone, rain drop, and air molecule.
Example 5.4 demonstrates that a bullet losing 90% of its kinetic energy loses only about 68% of its speed.
Work done by a variable force is calculated by summing the work done over small displacements where the force is approximately constant.
The total work done is the limit of the sum of F(x)Δx as Δx approaches zero, which is equivalent to the definite integral of F(x) dx.
The work done by a variable force is equal to the area under the force-displacement curve.
